records.sourceFile: Establishing weighted criteria for return to play after hamstring injury - a systematic review and methodological quality analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Bru-Ruiz JJ, Pérez-Cruzado D, García-Romero J, Ruiz-Muñoz M, Canca-Sánchez JC, González-Sanchez M. Establishing weighted criteria for return to play after hamstring injury: a systematic review and methodological quality analysis. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2026;27:777.
paper.abstract: The authors searched four databases for studies on criteria to return hamstring-injured athletes to activity and report pain as the most common criterion. They recommend combining pain with strength, flexibility and sport-specific movement at maximum speed. The abstract reports 22 included studies, while the results section reports 26.
paper.tldr: Pain is still the most common return criterion after hamstring injury, and the authors suggest pairing it with strength and flexibility within about 10% of the uninjured leg, plus sport-specific maximum-speed tests. The included studies are small and uneven in quality, and the authors call for standardized criteria, so use these as a checklist to discuss rather than fixed cut-offs.
paper.methods: This PRISMA-guided systematic review was registered on OSF, with the searches run on 20 April 2026 and no filters applied beyond five publication languages. Two reviewers screened blind in Rayyan (kappa 0.81, rising to 0.96 after discussion), appraising trials with PEDro, observational studies with STROBE and reviews with PRISMA. The authors then weighted each criterion by evidence level, internal validity and clinical consensus or relapse prediction, and presented the result as a hierarchy diagram.
paper.findings: Pain was the most common criterion: 10 of the 12 studies that addressed it favored absence of pain and 2 opposed its use. All 8 studies that analyzed functional tests supported them, while imaging was the least favored criterion (3 supported it and 6 opposed it). The authors describe a maximum 10% deficit against the uninjured limb for strength and flexibility as a consensus, drawn from a handful of included studies, and report that De Vos et al. linked pain on palpation at return to almost four times the relapse risk.
paper.limitations: The authors acknowledge heterogeneous study designs, inconsistent methodological quality and little standardization of instruments and thresholds. The abstract's 22 studies conflicts with the 26 in the results, and the text's 13 primary studies appear as 11 in Table 4. The search used only hamstring terms, although the Strengths section calls it the first review of return criteria for lower-limb injuries, and the weighting is author judgment rather than a validated method.
paper.practicalImplications: Build return decisions from several measures rather than pain alone, and record the exact instrument and test protocol, which the authors found often unreported. Where pre-injury data are missing, use the uninjured limb as the reference, which the authors describe as the more practical and reproducible option.
paper.athleteDev: Treat return-to-play testing as a profile of pain, strength, flexibility and maximum-speed or sport-specific movement, each compared with the uninjured leg. The review gives no validated thresholds, so the 10% limb deficit and the 60 m sprint result within 2% of pre-injury (from one 12-athlete sprinter cohort, Otsuka et al. 2022) should be starting points for local data, not cut-offs.
paper.rtp: The review supports using pain, limb-to-limb strength and flexibility, and functional tests together when deciding return to sport after hamstring injury. It cannot set a validated cut-off or show that any single criterion predicts re-injury: the authors say no consensus exists, a secondary review they cite reports that none of the return criteria have been validated, and the relapse risk estimates, such as about 4% higher relapse risk per newton of strength lost, come from one 64-patient trial (De Vos et al. 2014).

records.sourceFile: Are There Sex Disparities in Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction_ A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Elliott DA, Gill SS, Gupte CM. Are There Sex Disparities in Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction? A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis. Am J Sports Med. 2026;54(12):3070-3080.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of 25 studies (7,183 athletes) comparing return to sport after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction between males and females. Female athletes had lower odds of return to sport at 12 and up to 24 months, with no significant sex difference for return to competition, return to preinjury level or time to return.
paper.tldr: Female athletes were less likely than male athletes to be back in sport in the first two years after primary ACL reconstruction, but long-term return rates and time to return were similar. The pooled data are exploratory and observational, so they flag a midterm gap worth monitoring rather than proving that sex-specific programs are needed.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science from inception to 27 September 2025, including primary studies that compared return to sport by sex after primary ACL reconstruction with outcomes at 12 months of follow-up. Exploratory random-effects meta-analysis (Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios; mean differences for time to return), with risk of bias assessed by ROBINS-I; protocol registered in PROSPERO.
paper.findings: Female athletes had lower odds of return to sport at 12 months (8 studies; OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62-0.92) and up to and including 24 months (16 studies; OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.61-0.85). At exactly 24 months (5 studies; OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.44-1.06) and at the longest follow-up (24 studies; OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.63-1.07) the differences were not significant. Time to return did not differ (7 studies; mean difference 0.48 months, 95% CI -0.19 to 1.14), and there was no sex difference for return to competition or return to preinjury level.
paper.limitations: All studies were at serious risk of bias from confounding and 24 of 25 were at serious overall risk, with most being cohort, cross-sectional or case-series designs. Return-to-sport definitions, graft types and sports varied, sex-stratified data were scarce, and psychological and hormonal variables were not measured consistently. The text labels two separate analyses 'At 24 months'; the 16-study OR 0.72 matches the abstract's 'up to and including 24 months' result.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can expect female athletes to be somewhat less likely than male athletes to be back in sport within the first two years after primary ACL reconstruction, while time to return and long-term return look similar. The authors call for sex-specific rehabilitation and psychological support, but the review did not test any such intervention.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not support different return timelines or performance targets by sex, because time to return and return to preinjury level did not differ. Its use for performance staff is limited to knowing that fewer female athletes may be back in sport during the midterm window.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport planning after primary ACL reconstruction: female athletes had lower odds of being back in sport at 12 to 24 months, with no difference at longest follow-up. It cannot set individual return criteria or timelines, and it does not test any rehabilitation or psychological intervention.

records.sourceFile: Return-to-Sport Outcomes and Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Revision Compared to the Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Manojlovic M, Milankov V, Roklicer R, Trivic T, Veraksa A, Bianco A, et al. Return-to-Sport Outcomes and Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Revision Compared to the Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:47.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 observational studies (3,209 athletes) comparing revision and primary ACL reconstruction on return to sport, return at preinjury competition level, time to return and psychological readiness. Revision was associated with slightly lower return rates, a slightly longer return and moderately lower psychological readiness, all at very low certainty.
paper.tldr: After revision ACL reconstruction, athletes returned to sport and to their preinjury level slightly less often (about 5 to 6 percentage points), took about 1.2 months longer, and reported lower psychological readiness than after primary reconstruction. The evidence is observational and very low certainty, so treat these as planning expectations, not fixed effects.
paper.methods: Search of Web of Science, EMBASE and PubMed for English-language studies from January 2015 to October 2024, updated on 15 November 2024, for observational studies comparing revision and primary ACL reconstruction (at least 10 patients per group). Quality was assessed with MINORS and certainty with GRADE; odds ratios and standardized mean differences were pooled in RevMan with fixed- and random-effects (Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman) models; registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024600347).
paper.findings: Revision patients had lower odds of return to sport (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.49-0.89; I2 = 16%) and of return at the preinjury competition level (43% vs 48%; OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.36-0.76; I2 = 55%). Time to return was 1.2 months longer (SMD 0.38; p = 0.004; I2 = 69%), and ACL-RSI psychological readiness was about 14.2 points lower (SMD -0.75, 95% CI -1.14 to -0.36; I2 = 81%). Mean MINORS score was 16.7 (moderate quality) and GRADE certainty was very low for all outcomes.
paper.limitations: Only observational studies were included, revision samples were small relative to primary samples (830 vs 2,736 reported, which sums to more than the stated 3,209 total), and data on sex, graft type, sport and level of play were too limited to analyze. The time-to-return CI is printed as '0.12 to -0.63' in the abstract and results, and the sensitivity result as '0.18 to -0.69', so the upper bounds appear to have a sign error (presumably 0.63 and 0.69). Psychological readiness rests on only three studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing an athlete after revision ACL reconstruction can expect a slightly lower chance of returning to sport and to the preinjury competition level, a slightly longer timeline, and lower psychological readiness than after primary reconstruction. The authors recommend combining exercise and psychological interventions after revision, but this recommendation was not tested in the review.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can allow for a slightly longer timeline and lower readiness when setting goals after revision reconstruction, and should not assume a return to preinjury level. The review gives very low certainty group averages, so it cannot set targets for an individual athlete.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport planning after revision ACL reconstruction: lower odds of return and of return at preinjury level, about 1.2 months longer to return, and lower ACL-RSI scores. It cannot set individual return criteria, and it does not show whether any rehabilitation or psychological protocol improves outcomes after revision.

records.sourceFile: Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.pdf

paper.citation: Chen J, Wu Y, Xu H, Ren Y, Yang R, Yao S, et al. Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Front Physiol. 2026;17:1792091.
paper.abstract: Network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (n = 797) comparing resistance training modalities after primary ACL reconstruction on quadriceps strength, quadriceps mass, knee function and health-related quality of life, using SUCRA rankings and GRADE. BFRT had the most consistent benefit for quadriceps strength and mass versus usual rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: Blood flow restriction training was the only modality with moderate certainty evidence of better quadriceps strength and mass than usual rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction. Rankings for knee function (isokinetic) and quality of life (eccentric) are very low certainty and should be treated as provisional.
paper.methods: Searches of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science and Google Scholar to 30 September 2025 for English-language randomized trials in adults or adolescents after primary ACL reconstruction comparing modality-dominant resistance training with standard multimodal rehabilitation or with each other. Frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of standardized mean differences with SUCRA rankings, RoB 2 risk of bias, design-by-treatment and node-splitting consistency checks, and GRADE for network comparisons; registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251182456).
paper.findings: For quadriceps strength (18 trials, 693 participants) BFRT ranked first (SUCRA 81.7; SMD 0.40, 95% CI 0.07-0.73 vs usual rehabilitation), and for quadriceps mass (10 trials, 293 participants) BFRT ranked first (SUCRA 79.1; SMD 0.82, 95% CI 0.11-1.53), both moderate certainty. For knee function (10 trials, 339 participants) isokinetic training ranked highest (SUCRA 87.7) but no pairwise difference was significant. For quality of life (7 trials, 173 participants) eccentric training ranked first (SUCRA 87.4; SMD 1.31, 95% CI 0.01-2.63, p = 0.050), with very low certainty and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 73.5%).
paper.limitations: The network was uneven, with only 3 isokinetic and 2 plyometric trials, and knee function and quality of life comparisons were all rated very low certainty. Cuff pressures, loading schemes, outcome instruments, time since surgery and graft type varied or were inconsistently reported, and most outcomes were measured immediately after the intervention. Risk of bias was low in 14 trials and some concerns in 8.
paper.practicalImplications: BFRT can be considered when the main goal is quadriceps strength or size recovery, since it beat usual rehabilitation at moderate certainty. Eccentric training for quality of life and isokinetic training for knee function are very low certainty signals, and the comparator was usual rehabilitation that often already included strengthening.
paper.athleteDev: Rehabilitation and performance staff can use BFRT as a supported option for early quadriceps recovery after ACL reconstruction. The review does not test sport-specific performance outcomes such as sprinting, jumping or change of direction.
paper.rtp: Relevant to rehabilitation after primary ACL reconstruction, where BFRT improved quadriceps strength and mass versus usual rehabilitation. The review does not measure time to return to sport, sport readiness or re-injury, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return.

records.sourceFile: Platelet-Rich Plasma Accelerates the Return to Sport in Athletes with Acute Muscle Injuries - A Systematic Review and Statistical Fragility Index-Based Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.pdf

paper.citation: Bensa A, Fattini Fellini G, Boffa A, Grassi A, Samuelsson K, Filardo G. Platelet-Rich Plasma Accelerates the Return to Sport in Athletes with Acute Muscle Injuries: A Systematic Review and Statistical Fragility Index-Based Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:55.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and fragility-index meta-analysis of nine randomized trials (474 patients) comparing platelet-rich plasma injections with rehabilitation or placebo for acute muscle injuries. PRP shortened time to return to sport, improved pain only in hamstring trials, and did not change re-injury or complications.
paper.tldr: In nine small trials, platelet-rich plasma injections shortened return to sport after acute muscle injury by about a week compared with control, mostly in hamstring injuries. Certainty is low and the effect varied widely between trials, so treat PRP as an option to discuss with the physician, not a standard step.
paper.methods: PRISMA review (PROSPERO CRD42024545885) searching PubMed, Cochrane Library and Web of Science on 6 January 2026 for English-language RCTs comparing PRP injection with rehabilitation or placebo for acute muscle injury. Outcomes were time to return to sport, VAS pain, re-injury and complications, with sub-analyses of double-blind and hamstring-only trials; data were pooled with DerSimonian-Laird random effects (MD) and the Peto method (OR), robustness was tested with the fragility index and continuous fragility index, and quality was rated with RoB 2 and GRADE.
paper.findings: PRP shortened return to sport by 7.5 days overall (9 RCTs, 458 analysed, p < 0.001, CFI 188), 8.8 days in double-blind trials (4 RCTs, 217 patients, CFI 67) and 7.5 days in hamstring trials (6 RCTs, 299 patients, CFI 97). VAS pain did not differ overall (5 RCTs) or in double-blind trials, but improved by 0.4 points with PRP in three hamstring trials (p = 0.006), which the authors call of limited clinical relevance. Re-injury (7 RCTs, FI 5, 'slightly fragile') and complications (9 RCTs, FI 7) did not differ, and strength, imaging and function were mostly similar between groups in the few trials reporting them.
paper.limitations: Few trials and patients, five at high risk of bias, very high heterogeneity for overall return to sport (I2 92%) and wide variation in PRP preparation, injection number, volume, lesion size and site. Comparators differed (rehabilitation alone, saline, Traumeel, hematoma evacuation), and return-to-sport criteria are not described. The discussion says the double-blind sub-analysis confirmed the VAS result, but the results report no significant VAS difference in that subgroup.
paper.practicalImplications: For acute hamstring or other muscle injuries, PRP is an option the medical team may discuss, with pooled trials showing about a week faster return and no added re-injury or complications. Given low certainty and wide variation between trials, it should not replace a criteria-based rehabilitation plan.
paper.athleteDev: Limited direct use for performance staff: the review reports time to return and pain, not strength recovery or performance after return. Rehabilitation timelines should still be driven by the athlete's progress, with PRP at most a possible shortening factor.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport timing after acute muscle injury, mainly hamstring injury, where pooled trials favoured PRP by about a week. It cannot tell staff when an athlete is ready to return, how they perform afterwards, or whether PRP changes re-injury risk, which did not differ in these trials.

records.sourceFile: Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes after ankle syndesmosis injuries - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Li R, Sun C, Qi P, Xu Z. Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes after ankle syndesmosis injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Surg Res. 2026;21:69.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies (901 elite athletes) with ankle syndesmosis injuries, pooling return-to-sport rate and summarising time to return. Pooled return to match play was 96%, with similar rates after suture-button fixation and nonoperative management, and time to return averaged about 58 days across studies.
paper.tldr: Almost all professional and collegiate athletes in these studies returned to match play after an ankle syndesmosis injury (pooled 96%). Return time depended heavily on severity and treatment, from about two weeks for stable sprains managed without surgery to three or four months after surgical fixation.
paper.methods: PRISMA review (PROSPERO CRD420251149156) searching PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library to September 2025 for cohort studies, RCTs and case series reporting return to sport in elite or professional athletes with syndesmosis injury. Return rates were pooled with logit-transformed random-effects models in R, with subgroup, leave-one-out and meta-regression analyses; quality was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, certainty with GRADE, and publication bias with funnel plots and Egger's test.
paper.findings: Pooled return to match play was 96% (95% CI 93-98%), 98% for suture-button fixation (95% CI 92-99%) and 98% for nonoperative management (95% CI 94-99%), with 90% (95% CI 83-95%) in studies not reporting treatment (subgroup difference p = 0.014). Leaving out the large NFL cohort raised the pooled rate to 98% with no heterogeneity. Time to return, reported in 13 studies, averaged about 58 days unweighted (range 13-133), with Table 1 showing roughly 13 to 45 days in nonoperative studies and 41 to 133 days in suture-button studies.
paper.limitations: Studies were mostly retrospective and observational with limited control of confounding, and publication bias suggests the pooled rate may be overestimated. Time to return lacked variability measures, so the 58-day figure is an unweighted descriptive average with limited inferential value. Treatment groups differ in injury grade (stable injuries treated nonoperatively, unstable injuries fixed), so similar return rates do not show the treatments are interchangeable; the abstract says five databases while the methods list four.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes with a syndesmosis injury can be told that return to match play is very likely, but the expected timeline should be set by injury grade and treatment rather than a single average. In these studies stable, low-grade injuries managed nonoperatively returned in weeks, while high-grade injuries needing fixation took about two to four months.
paper.athleteDev: Limited direct use for performance staff beyond planning: the review reports whether and roughly when athletes returned, not performance after return or the rehabilitation content. Use the severity- and treatment-specific ranges from the study table, not the overall 58-day average, when planning an athlete's absence.
paper.rtp: Relevant to expectation setting after syndesmosis injury in professional and collegiate athletes: nearly all returned to match play. It cannot set clearance criteria or an individual timeline, because return time was not pooled and return to pre-injury performance level was not assessed.
